opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I used to say that, and I said it pretty loudly. A few years ago my take was that quadrotors were basically a solved problem. We had good dynamics models, mature controllers, solid state estimation, and you could buy a platform off the shelf that flew beautifully. So I'd tell students: if you want impact, go work on manipulation or legged robots, where the open problems are.

What changed my mind was seeing where the field actually went. "Solved" was true for a narrow slice: hovering, following a trajectory in a motion-capture room, flying in a clean environment. Once you move into the real world, a lot opens back up. Think of agile flight through cluttered spaces using only onboard sensing, flying near people or obstacles where you need real safety guarantees, or physically interacting with the environment, like perching, pushing, carrying things, or doing aerial manipulation. Those are hard, unsolved problems.

The second thing was learning. When people started combining reinforcement learning and learned perception with the strong physics-based models we already had for quadrotors, the drone turned out to be an almost ideal testbed. The dynamics are fast and unforgiving, so you find out right away whether your method works. And the simulation-to-reality gap is small enough that you can iterate quickly, yet large enough to be interesting. Some of the clearest demonstrations of learned control beating hand-designed approaches came from aerial robots.

So my view now is not "stop working on quadrotors." It's "stop working on the parts we already understand." If a student wants to do one more trajectory-tracking paper in a mocap arena, I'd still push back. But if they want to use the quadrotor as a platform to study autonomy, learning, or safety under real constraints, I think it's one of the best places to be. I was wrong to treat the hardware as the research question. The interesting question is what the robot can do on its own in a messy world, and that's far from settled.

r001.rationale: The response says quadrotor engineering is mature but research opportunities remain in autonomy, learning, safety, and interaction, distinguishing the hardware’s maturity from the platform’s remaining research value.

r002.rationale: It describes mature dynamics models, controllers, state estimation, and off-the-shelf platforms, then explains that researchers can build on those foundations while studying harder problems.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. Honestly, I think I was wrong, or at least I was only half right. When I said students should stop researching quadrotors, what I was really reacting to was a specific kind of work: another slightly different controller, another trajectory planner that is a few percent smoother, another paper that flies through a slightly smaller gap. The platform was so mature that a lot of research had turned into incremental benchmarking, and I worried that students were spending years on problems where the ceiling was already visible.

Two things changed my mind.

The first is that I underestimated how much the quadrotor is a vehicle for ideas rather than the idea itself. If you want to test a new learning-based perception method, or a new way of reasoning about uncertainty, or a new approach to real-time safety guarantees, you need a platform that is cheap, fast, dangerous enough to be honest, and easy to instrument. Nothing else checks all those boxes the way a quadrotor does. So telling students to leave quadrotors was, in effect, telling them to give up one of the best experimental testbeds we have. That was a bad trade.

The second is that the field moved under me. A few years ago, the hard problems looked solved on paper, but the moment you put these systems outdoors, in wind, with degraded GPS, with unreliable vision, in a swarm, they fell apart. Those failures are where the interesting research is now. Robust autonomy in the real world, long-duration operation, interaction with people, learning from very little data: those are not quadrotor problems, they are robotics problems, and the quadrotor just happens to be the fastest way to expose them.

So my advice today is different. Don't research quadrotors as the goal. Research a hard question, and if a quadrotor is the sharpest tool for asking it, use it without apology. What I was really saying before, and said badly, was: don't let the platform pick your problem for you.

r001.rationale: The response separates the quadrotor’s maturity as an engineered platform from its continuing value as a testbed for new research ideas and real-world robotics problems.

r002.rationale: It describes quadrotors as cheap, fast, and easy to instrument, but does not explain that established engineering foundations spare researchers from re-solving basic implementation problems.

astra-6.text: I used to think students should move on because quadrotors were already so well studied. But I realized I was confusing the platform with the research question. Getting a quadrotor to fly is one thing; getting it to operate reliably in an unfamiliar environment is another. The important question is whether you’re using that platform to explore something new. So I changed my view: students shouldn’t avoid quadrotors just because people have worked on them for years. They should avoid repeating work without asking what new insight they’re contributing.

r001.rationale: The response separates basic flight from new research questions and says years of prior work do not exhaust quadrotors’ value as platforms.

r002.rationale: It does not explain that established engineering foundations let researchers focus on research without re-solving basic implementation problems.

sol-6.1.text: I used to think quadrotors were becoming a solved problem, so students should move on to something else. But that confuses having a platform that works with having answered all the interesting research questions. Getting a quadrotor to fly is one thing; getting it to operate reliably in unfamiliar environments, with limited sensing and real uncertainty, is another. So I’d revise that advice: don’t stop researching quadrotors—make sure you’re asking a meaningful question, rather than just building another flying demo.

r001.rationale: It distinguishes getting a quadrotor to fly from answering the remaining interesting research questions.

r002.rationale: It says the platform can work, but does not explain that established engineering foundations let researchers focus on research without re-solving basic implementation problems.
